arrays-hashing.name: Arrays & Hashing
signals: “have I seen this element before?” → hash set
pair/count/group lookups → hash map keyed by value, count, or a canonical form (sorted string, tuple)
“sum of a range” many times → prefix sums
arrays-hashing.one_liner: The toolbox everything else builds on: trade memory for O(1) lookups. Most “clever” array problems are a hash map with the right key, or a prefix-sum identity like sum(i..j) = pre[j+1] - pre[i].
template: # two-sum shape: one pass, check the complement before inserting

subtopics.name: Hash set & map basics
subtopics.recognize: “Have I seen this before?”, “does a pair exist?”, O(1) membership or key→value bookkeeping.
subtopics.solve: One pass; query the map before inserting the current element so each pair is seen exactly once.

subtopics.name: Grouping & counting
subtopics.recognize: “Group the equivalent items”, “most frequent”, “appears more than n/k times”.
subtopics.solve: Map from a canonical key (sorted string, count signature) to a bucket; counts via Counter. Majority element has the O(1)-space Boyer-Moore vote.

subtopics.name: Prefix sums & products
subtopics.recognize: Many range-sum queries, “subarray summing to k” (negatives allowed!), “product of everything except me”.
subtopics.solve: pre[i+1] = pre[i] + a[i], so sum(i..j) = pre[j+1] - pre[i]. Count subarrays with a map of previously seen prefix values; “except self” = prefix pass × suffix pass.
template: # subarrays summing to k (works with negatives)

subtopics.name: Difference arrays
subtopics.recognize: Many range updates (+v on [l, r]), one final read of the whole array.
subtopics.solve: d[l] += v and d[r+1] -= v per update; a prefix sum over d recovers the values. Car pooling and flight bookings are this.
template: for l, r, v in updates:

subtopics.name: In-place array surgery
subtopics.recognize: “Do it in O(1) extra space”: remove/keep elements, partition by value, find the missing one by using the array itself.
subtopics.solve: Slow writer + fast reader, or cyclic swaps that park value v at index v. Sort Colors is a 3-way partition with two boundaries.

subtopics.name: String scanning & run grouping
subtopics.recognize: Format, split, align, or match strings; no algorithmic depth, all edge cases.
subtopics.solve: Walk the string once with clear state; build results in a list and join. Rehearse these — interviewers use them to check clean code speed.

subtopics.name: Sorting & simulation
subtopics.recognize: “Design a structure”, “validate a board”, or a scan where sorting first makes the logic trivial.
subtopics.solve: Pick the invariant, then simulate carefully. GetRandom O(1) pairs a list with an index map; swap-with-last makes deletion O(1).

two-pointers.name: Two Pointers
signals: sorted array + “find a pair/triple” → opposite ends, move the pointer that helps
in-place remove/partition → slow writer + fast reader
linked-list cycle or middle → fast & slow pointers
two-pointers.one_liner: Two indices replace a nested loop because moving one pointer can never help the other side: O(n²) → O(n). Ask “when I look at a[l] and a[r], which side is provably useless now?”
template: elif s < target: l += 1     # a[l] can never pair with anything -> drop it

sliding-window.name: Sliding Window
signals: “longest/shortest contiguous subarray or substring such that …”
“max/min/count over every window of size k”
needs monotonicity: growing the window only makes the condition worse (or better)
sliding-window.one_liner: A moving window whose stats update incrementally: add the new right element, shrink from the left while the window is broken. Never recompute a window from scratch.

stack.name: Stack & Monotonic Stack
signals: matching/nesting (parentheses, undo, calculators) → plain stack
“next/previous greater (or smaller) element” → monotonic stack
“largest rectangle / trapped water / visible items” → monotonic stack
stack.one_liner: A stack remembers what is still waiting to be resolved. Keep it monotonic and each element is pushed and popped once: every “nearest element beating me” question in O(n).
template: j = st.pop()            # x is the next greater element of a[j]

subtopics.name: Matching & elimination
subtopics.recognize: Nested/paired symbols, collisions that cancel adjacent items, “generate all valid parentheses”.
subtopics.solve: Push what is unresolved; the stack top is always the most recent open item. Asteroid-style problems pop while the new element destroys the top. Generate Parentheses is backtracking on open/close counts.

subtopics.name: Expression parsing
subtopics.recognize: Evaluate or decode a string with operators, brackets, or repeat counts.
subtopics.solve: One stack for numbers and one for pending operators/context; on '(' push state, on ')' pop and combine. RPN is the pure form: push operands, apply operators.

subtopics.name: Monotonic stack
subtopics.recognize: “Next/previous greater (or smaller) element”, “days until warmer”, “largest rectangle”, spans.
subtopics.solve: Keep indices whose values are monotonic; each pop resolves one element's answer. Every element pushes and pops once: O(n).
template: j = st.pop()            # x is a[j]'s next greater element

subtopics.name: Stack & queue design
subtopics.recognize: “Design a stack/queue with an extra O(1) query” (min, max frequency), or build one container from another.
subtopics.solve: Store the auxiliary answer alongside each element (value, min-so-far), so pop restores it for free.

binary-search.name: Binary Search
signals: sorted (or rotated-sorted) input → search for a boundary, not just equality
“minimize the maximum / maximize the minimum / least k such that …” → binary search the answer
check(x) is monotonic: if x works, so does every larger x
binary-search.one_liner: Binary search needs monotonicity, not a sorted array. Frame everything as “first index where check() flips from false to true” and the off-by-ones disappear.
template: lo, hi = 0, n               # first x with check(x) true

subtopics.name: Boundary on sorted data
subtopics.recognize: Sorted input + “find the position / first / last occurrence”, or a store queried by timestamp.
subtopics.solve: Frame every variant as lower_bound: the first index where check() is true. Then first occurrence, insert position, and ranges are all the same code.
template: lo, hi = 0, n               # first index with check true

subtopics.name: Rotated & mountain arrays
subtopics.recognize: “Sorted then rotated”, “peak element”, “mountain array” — piecewise-sorted data.
subtopics.solve: Compare mid against an endpoint to decide which half is normally sorted, then decide which half can contain the target. Duplicates can force a linear step.

subtopics.name: Binary search the answer
subtopics.recognize: “Minimum speed/capacity/largest-sum so that …”, “minimize the maximum”. The answer itself is the search space.
subtopics.solve: check(x) = “is x feasible?” must be monotonic; binary search the smallest feasible x. sqrt(x) is the same idea on values.

subtopics.name: Divide & eliminate
subtopics.recognize: Two sorted arrays jointly (median), or a row+column-sorted matrix.
subtopics.solve: Median: binary search the partition of the shorter array. Sorted matrix: start at the top-right corner and discard a row or column each step.

linked-list.name: Linked List
signals: reverse / reorder / splice in place → prev-cur pointer surgery with a dummy head
cycle detection, middle, k-th from end → fast & slow pointers
“merge k lists” → heap of heads
linked-list.one_liner: Almost every list problem is careful pointer surgery. A dummy node kills the empty-list and head edge cases; draw the before/after arrows before coding.

subtopics.name: Reversal
subtopics.recognize: “Reverse the list / a sublist / in k-groups”, “swap pairs”.
subtopics.solve: The three-pointer loop below is the atom; sublist and k-group reversal wrap it with a dummy head and careful reconnection. Draw the arrows first.

subtopics.name: Dummy head & deletion
subtopics.recognize: Delete/skip/partition nodes where the head itself might be removed, “remove nth from end”, “rotate”.
subtopics.solve: dummy = ListNode(0, head) kills every head edge case. For nth-from-end, advance a lead pointer n steps, then move both.

subtopics.name: Fast & slow pointers
subtopics.recognize: Cycle? middle? intersection? palindrome? — questions about list SHAPE without extra space.
subtopics.solve: fast moves 2, slow moves 1: they meet iff there is a cycle; reset one to head and they meet at the cycle entrance. Middle = where fast hits the end. Duplicate-number is this on the array seen as a function graph.

subtopics.name: Merging & divide
subtopics.recognize: “Merge two/k sorted lists”, “sort a list”, “add two numbers”.
subtopics.solve: Two-list merge with a dummy tail is the atom; k lists use a heap of heads (or pairwise merging); sort = split at middle + merge (mergesort).

subtopics.name: Design & copying
subtopics.recognize: “Design LRU/LFU/circular queue”, “copy a list with random pointers”.
subtopics.solve: LRU = hashmap + doubly-linked list, evict the tail. Random-pointer copy: map old→new (or interleave copies in place).

trees.name: Trees & BSTs
signals: “for every node …” / path sums / depth / diameter → DFS returning info upward
“level by level / zigzag / rightmost per level” → BFS with a queue
BST → inorder is sorted; prune by comparing with the root
trees.one_liner: Trust the recursion: assume the recursive call already solves the subtree, then combine the children's answers at the root. Distinguish “answer passes through this node” from “answer returned to the parent”.
template: ans = max(ans, left + right)   # path through node
return max(left, right) + 1    # best chain up to parent

subtopics.name: Traversal basics
subtopics.recognize: “Return the in/pre/postorder”, “iterator over a BST”.
subtopics.solve: Know the recursive version cold and the stack-based iterative inorder (push all lefts, pop, go right) — the iterator is exactly that stack, paused.

subtopics.name: Top-down DFS (preorder)
subtopics.recognize: Info flows root→leaf: running path sum, max seen so far, “count good nodes”, root-to-leaf numbers.
subtopics.solve: Pass accumulators as parameters; check leaf conditions at the leaf.

subtopics.name: Bottom-up DFS (postorder)
subtopics.recognize: A node's answer depends on its children: height, balance, symmetry, same/subtree, invert, prune.
subtopics.solve: Trust the recursion: assume dfs(child) already answers the subtree, combine at the node, return upward.
template: return max(left, right) + 1   # combine children's answers

subtopics.name: BFS by level
subtopics.recognize: “Level order / zigzag / average per level / right side view / connect next pointers”.
subtopics.solve: Queue; loop len(q) times per level so levels stay separated. Right side view = last node of each level.

subtopics.name: BST property
subtopics.recognize: The tree is a BST: validate, k-th smallest, closest values, insert/delete, LCA by value.
subtopics.solve: Inorder is sorted — many BST problems are “inorder + observation”. Validation passes down (lo, hi) bounds. LCA: walk from root, split point is the answer.

subtopics.name: Build & transform
subtopics.recognize: “Construct from preorder+inorder”, serialize/deserialize, flatten, count complete-tree nodes.
subtopics.solve: Construction: the first preorder element is the root; inorder splits left/right (use an index map). Serialization: preorder with null markers.

subtopics.name: Paths & tree DP
subtopics.recognize: “Max path sum anywhere”, “count paths summing to k”, LCA of arbitrary nodes, rob houses on a tree.
subtopics.solve: Distinguish “best chain returned to parent” from “best path through the node” (diameter trick). Path Sum III = prefix sums on the root path. Tree DP returns a tuple of states per node.

heap.name: Heap / Priority Queue
signals: “top-k / k-th largest / k closest” → heap of size k
“running median” → two heaps balanced around the middle
repeatedly “take the smallest, put back something” → heap-driven simulation
heap.one_liner: A heap gives the current min (or max) in O(log n) without full sorting. For top-k, keep a min-heap of size k: the root is the k-th largest so far.
template: heapq.heappop(h)        # root of h = k-th largest

subtopics.name: Top-k & k-th
subtopics.recognize: “k largest/smallest/closest/most frequent”, “k-th element”, “k smallest pairs”.
subtopics.solve: Min-heap of size k: push, pop when over k; the root is the k-th largest. Quickselect gives O(n) average for a one-shot k-th.

subtopics.name: Two heaps
subtopics.recognize: “Running median”, or any “split the stream around the middle” question.
subtopics.solve: Max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper, rebalanced so sizes differ by ≤ 1; the median lives at the roots.

subtopics.name: Scheduling & rearranging
subtopics.recognize: Repeatedly take the best available item, possibly with cooldowns or capacities: tasks, stones, seats, “no two adjacent equal”.
subtopics.solve: Heap keyed by the greedy criterion (count, end time, ratio); pop, use, push back the updated item. Car Pooling is the simpler difference-array cousin.

backtracking.name: Backtracking
signals: “generate ALL combinations / permutations / partitions”
constraint satisfaction on a small n (n ≤ ~20): boards, digits, words
decision tree where each level chooses one element or position
backtracking.one_liner: Systematic exhaustive search: choose, explore, un-choose. Define what one level of the tree decides, then prune branches that already violate the constraints.

subtopics.name: Subsets & combinations
subtopics.recognize: “All subsets / combinations summing to target / letter combinations”. Order inside a choice does not matter.
subtopics.solve: Pass a start index so each element is considered once; reuse allowed → recurse with i, not i+1. Duplicates: sort, then skip a[i]==a[i-1] at the same depth.
template: ans.append(path[:])         # every node is a subset
if i > start and a[i] == a[i-1]: continue  # dup guard

subtopics.name: Permutations & boards
subtopics.recognize: “All orderings”, N-Queens style constraint boards. Order matters, each element used once.
subtopics.solve: Track a used[] set (or column/diagonal sets for queens); choose, recurse, un-choose. Duplicates: sort + skip equal values whose previous twin is unused.

subtopics.name: Partition backtracking
subtopics.recognize: “Split the string into valid pieces” (palindromes, dictionary words) and return all ways.
subtopics.solve: At position i, try every valid prefix and recurse on the rest; memoize feasibility when only counting or checking.

subtopics.name: Search with pruning
subtopics.recognize: Grid word search, bucket-filling into k equal groups, matchsticks — exponential search that lives or dies on pruning.
subtopics.solve: Prune hard: sort descending, skip equal buckets, bail when a bucket overflows. Mark grid cells visited in place and restore on backtrack.

tries.name: Tries
signals: many words + “starts with / prefix” queries
search a board or stream against a whole dictionary at once
wildcard letters → DFS over trie children
tries.one_liner: A tree keyed by characters: shared prefixes are stored once, so prefix queries cost O(len(word)) regardless of dictionary size.

subtopics.name: Build & query
subtopics.recognize: Many words + “insert / exact search / startsWith”.
subtopics.solve: Nested maps (or arrays of 26); walk character by character; '$' marks end-of-word.

subtopics.name: Wildcards & board search
subtopics.recognize: Search with '.' wildcards, or find MANY words in one grid at once.
subtopics.solve: Wildcard → DFS over all children at that node. Word Search II: DFS the grid while walking the trie, prune dead branches, remove found words.

subtopics.name: Trie + DP
subtopics.recognize: Partition/segment a string against a dictionary where prefix matching is the bottleneck.
subtopics.solve: f[i] over positions; transitions walk the trie from i instead of trying every substring.

graphs.name: Graphs
signals: “islands / connected regions / spread” on a grid → flood-fill DFS/BFS
shortest path with unit steps → BFS level by level
“prerequisites / build order” → topological sort
“are these connected / merge groups” → union-find
graphs.one_liner: Model the entities as nodes and relations as edges, then pick the traversal the question implies. A grid is just a graph whose neighbors are the 4 directions. Always mark visited when enqueuing, not when popping.
template: from collections import deque   # BFS shortest steps

subtopics.name: Grid flood fill (DFS)
subtopics.recognize: “Islands / regions / area / perimeter” on a grid; “spread from the border”.
subtopics.solve: DFS the 4 neighbors, mark visited by mutating the grid. Border-connected questions (Surrounded Regions, Pacific-Atlantic) flip the direction: start from the edges.
template: if not (0 <= r < R and 0 <= c < C) or g[r][c] != LAND: return 0

subtopics.name: BFS shortest steps
subtopics.recognize: “Minimum number of steps/mutations/moves”, “time for rot to spread” — unweighted shortest path, sometimes multi-source.
subtopics.solve: Queue + seen set; mark visited when ENQUEUING, not when popping. Multi-source: seed the queue with all sources at distance 0. Word Ladder builds neighbors via wildcard buckets.

subtopics.name: Topological sort
subtopics.recognize: “Prerequisites / build order / can you finish”, layered peeling (min height trees).
subtopics.solve: Kahn: queue of indegree-0 nodes, pop and decrement neighbors. Processed < n ⇒ cycle. Min Height Trees peels leaves layer by layer — same loop.
template: q = deque([u for u in range(n) if indeg[u] == 0])

subtopics.name: Graph modeling & traversal
subtopics.recognize: The graph is implicit: clone a graph, ratio queries along paths (evaluate division), degree puzzles (town judge).
subtopics.solve: Build the adjacency list first, then plain DFS/BFS. Some “graph” problems are only degree counting.

subtopics.name: Union-Find
subtopics.recognize: “Merge accounts / components”, “which edge creates a cycle”, connectivity as edges arrive.
subtopics.solve: DSU with path compression: find(x) follows parents; union attaches one root under the other. Count components by counting roots.

advanced-graphs.name: Advanced Graphs
signals: shortest path with weighted edges → Dijkstra (no negatives)
“connect everything at minimum cost” → minimum spanning tree
≤ k stops / negative edges → Bellman-Ford style relaxation
advanced-graphs.one_liner: Same graphs, weighted questions. Dijkstra is BFS with a priority queue: settle the closest unsettled node, relax its edges; stale heap entries are skipped when popped.
template: if d > dist.get(u, inf): continue   # stale

subtopics.name: Dijkstra, Floyd & minimax paths
subtopics.recognize: Shortest path with WEIGHTED edges (no negatives); “path minimizing the maximum edge” (effort, rising water); “cheapest flights within k stops”.
subtopics.solve: Heap of (dist, node); settle the closest, relax edges, skip stale pops. Minimax: replace + with max in the relaxation. K-stops caps the relaxation rounds (Bellman-Ford flavor).
template: if d > dist.get(u, inf): continue   # stale

subtopics.name: Minimum spanning tree
subtopics.recognize: “Connect all points at minimum total cost”.
subtopics.solve: Kruskal: sort edges, union-find, take edges that join two components. Critical edge = MST cost rises without it.

subtopics.name: Special structures
subtopics.recognize: Use-every-edge-once itineraries (Eulerian path), building a matrix from order constraints, connectivity through shared prime factors.
subtopics.solve: Eulerian: Hierholzer — DFS consuming edges, append on the way out, reverse. Order constraints → topological sort per axis. Shared-factor connectivity → union nodes with their prime factors.

dp-1d.name: 1-D Dynamic Programming
signals: “how many ways / min cost / max value” over a sequence → not the ways themselves
current choice depends on a few previous positions (climb stairs, rob houses)
“best subarray ending here” → Kadane
dp-1d.one_liner: Define f[i] = answer for the prefix ending at i, write the transition from smaller states, set base cases. If the recursive version overlaps subproblems, memoize it — that IS the DP.
template: # house-robber shape: take a[i] + f[i-2], or skip -> f[i-1]
f0, f1 = f1, max(f1, f0 + x)

subtopics.name: Linear transitions
subtopics.recognize: “How many ways to reach step n”, cost to climb, Fibonacci-shaped recurrences, counting with order (Combination Sum IV).
subtopics.solve: f[i] from f[i-1], f[i-2], …; roll two variables when only the last few states matter.

subtopics.name: Take or skip (House Robber)
subtopics.recognize: Pick elements under a no-two-adjacent constraint, maximize the total.
subtopics.solve: f[i] = max(f[i-1], f[i-2] + a[i]). Circular version: run twice, excluding the first or the last house.

subtopics.name: Best subarray ending here (Kadane)
subtopics.recognize: “Maximum product/sum subarray” — contiguous, best ending at each index.
subtopics.solve: Carry the best (and for products, the worst — negatives flip) subarray ending at i; answer is the best over all i.

subtopics.name: Partition & decode
subtopics.recognize: “Can the string be segmented / how many decodings / longest valid prefix structure”.
subtopics.solve: f[i] = answer for the first i chars; transitions try every valid last piece (dictionary word, 1-2 digit code).

subtopics.name: Knapsack
subtopics.recognize: “Fewest coins / perfect squares to build n”, “split into two equal halves”, “ways to hit a target with +/− signs”. Items combined under a capacity.
subtopics.solve: 0-1 knapsack: loop capacity DOWNWARD (each item once). Unbounded (coins): loop capacity upward. Counting uses +=. Target Sum reduces to subset-sum via (total + target) / 2.
template: for c in range(target, x - 1, -1):   # downward: use x once

subtopics.name: Subsequences & palindromes
subtopics.recognize: “Longest increasing subsequence”, “count palindromic substrings”.
subtopics.solve: LIS: patience trick — binary search a tails array, O(n log n). Palindromes: expand around each of the 2n−1 centers.

subtopics.name: Game DP
subtopics.recognize: Two players alternate taking from a line, both optimal, “who wins / best margin”.
subtopics.solve: f[i] = best score difference for the player to move from state i; take max over moves of (gain − f[next]).

dp-2d.name: 2-D Dynamic Programming
signals: two sequences compared (edit distance, LCS, interleaving) → f[i][j] on two prefixes
grid paths with costs/counts → f[r][c] from top/left
“pick items under a budget” → knapsack over (item, capacity)
dp-2d.one_liner: State = a pair of prefixes (or position + resource). Fill the table so every transition reads already-computed cells; for 0-1 knapsack compress to 1-D by looping capacity downward.

subtopics.name: Grid paths & submatrices
subtopics.recognize: Count/min-cost paths moving right+down, largest square, longest increasing path.
subtopics.solve: f[r][c] from top/left neighbors, row by row. Maximal square: f = min of three neighbors + 1. Arbitrary-direction grids → memoized DFS.

subtopics.name: Two sequences
subtopics.recognize: Compare two strings: LCS, edit distance, interleaving, distinct subsequences, regex matching.
subtopics.solve: f[i][j] = answer for prefixes s[:i], t[:j]; match ⇒ diagonal, else best of dropping a character from either side.
template: for i in range(1, m + 1):        # LCS

subtopics.name: State machines (stock series)
subtopics.recognize: Buy/sell with limits, cooldowns, or k transactions.
subtopics.solve: States = (day, holding?, transactions used); f transitions buy/sell/rest. All five stock problems are this one machine with different constraints.

subtopics.name: Interval DP
subtopics.recognize: “Burst balloons” — the answer for a range depends on choosing the LAST action inside it.
subtopics.solve: f[l][r] over gaps, lengths increasing; pick the last balloon k: f[l][r] = max over k of f[l][k] + f[k][r] + gain(l,k,r).

subtopics.name: Game DP on ranges
subtopics.recognize: Two players pick from ends/piles, both optimal.
subtopics.solve: f[l][r] = best margin for the mover on that range; or exploit parity (Stone Game I: first player always wins).

subtopics.name: Bitmask DP
subtopics.recognize: n ≤ ~20 and the state is “which elements are used”.
subtopics.solve: f[mask] = best over the last element added; iterate masks upward, transitions flip one bit.
template: f[mask] = min(f[mask], f[mask ^ (1 << i)] + cost(mask, i))

greedy.name: Greedy
signals: “minimum number of jumps/refuels/removals” where one obvious best move exists
sorting the input first makes the choice safe
an exchange argument shows a local choice never hurts the global optimum
greedy.one_liner: Commit to the locally best choice and never look back — valid only when you can argue no future regret (exchange argument). If you cannot argue it, it is probably DP.
template: if i > far: return False    # gap we can never cross

subtopics.name: Jump frontier
subtopics.recognize: “Can you reach the end / fewest jumps”, reachability with per-index ranges.
subtopics.solve: Sweep once, keep the furthest reachable index; count a jump when you pass the current frontier. BFS-on-intervals intuition.
template: if i > far: return False    # unreachable gap

subtopics.name: Running scans (Kadane family)
subtopics.recognize: “Maximum subarray”, circular variant, longest turbulent run.
subtopics.solve: Best subarray ending here: cur = max(x, cur + x). Circular = max(normal, total − minimum subarray). Turbulent: extend or restart the run per comparison sign.

subtopics.name: Partition by last occurrence
subtopics.recognize: “Cut into as many parts as possible so parts don't share letters”, build a target from pieces.
subtopics.solve: Precompute each element's last position; extend the current part to cover it; cut when i reaches the boundary.

subtopics.name: Exchange arguments & case analysis
subtopics.recognize: “Does a valid order/assignment exist”, distribute under fairness (candy), make change, circular gas tour.
subtopics.solve: Sort or scan with the one safe local rule, then prove no regret: gas station restarts after any failed prefix; candy needs a left pass + right pass.

intervals.name: Intervals
signals: “merge / insert / count overlapping intervals”
“minimum rooms / arrows / removals” over ranges
events with start & end → sort by one endpoint and sweep
intervals.one_liner: Sort, then sweep: after sorting by start, an interval overlaps the current merged block iff its start ≤ the block's end. For min-removals style questions, sort by END and greedily keep the earliest-ending interval.

subtopics.name: Merge & insert
subtopics.recognize: “Merge overlapping intervals”, “insert and merge”, “summarize ranges”.
subtopics.solve: Sort by start; overlap iff start ≤ current end; extend or push a new block.

subtopics.name: Sort by end (scheduling)
subtopics.recognize: “Fewest removals so none overlap”, “fewest arrows to pop all balloons”.
subtopics.solve: Sort by END and greedily keep the earliest-ending interval — it leaves the most room. Arrows = count the non-overlapping groups.

subtopics.name: Sweep with a heap
subtopics.recognize: Rooms/machines over time, per-query smallest covering interval.
subtopics.solve: Sort events; heap holds active intervals keyed by end (or size). Offline trick: sort queries too and answer them in order.

math-bits.name: Math & Bit Manipulation
signals: “without using +/×”, single number among pairs → XOR tricks
count bits / powers of two → n & (n-1) drops the lowest set bit
rotate/spiral/simulate a matrix → index mapping, layer by layer
math-bits.one_liner: A small bag of identities does the work: x ^ x = 0 (pairs cancel), n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit, rotate = transpose + reverse rows. Simulation problems reward careful index bookkeeping over cleverness.

subtopics.name: Bit tricks
subtopics.recognize: “Without +”, “single number among pairs/triples”, count bits, missing number.
subtopics.solve: x ^ x = 0 cancels pairs; n & (n-1) drops the lowest set bit; add = XOR + shifted carries. Triples: count each bit position mod 3.

subtopics.name: Bit by bit
subtopics.recognize: Sums over pairs of AND/OR/XOR, “maximum XOR”, constraints on which bits can be set.
subtopics.solve: Bits are independent: count how many numbers have bit b set and add its contribution separately. Maximum XOR builds the answer from the top bit down with a set or a trie.
template: ones = sum(x >> b & 1 for x in a)
ans += (1 << b) * ones * (n - ones)   # pairs whose XOR has bit b

subtopics.name: Numbers & digits
subtopics.recognize: Digit-by-digit arithmetic (reverse, plus one, add binary, multiply strings), gcd, factorial zeros, base conversions, digit cycles.
subtopics.solve: Simulate school arithmetic with explicit carries; gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a%b); trailing zeros = count factors of 5. Watch overflow rules the problem states.

subtopics.name: Matrix simulation
subtopics.recognize: Rotate / spiral / set zeroes / Game of Life — transform a grid, often in place.
subtopics.solve: Rotate = transpose + reverse each row. Spiral: four shrinking boundaries. In-place updates encode old+new state in the same cell (extra bit).

subtopics.name: Geometry & counting
subtopics.recognize: Points on a line, counting axis-aligned squares.
subtopics.solve: Fix one point, hash slopes in lowest terms. Squares: store point counts, iterate diagonal partners.

subtopics.name: Randomized algorithms
subtopics.recognize: “Pick uniformly at random” from a stream or by weight, shuffle in place.
subtopics.solve: Fisher-Yates shuffle; reservoir sampling keeps item i with probability 1/i; weighted pick = prefix sums + binary search.

insight.name: Insight & Case Analysis
signals: the constraints are tiny or huge in a way that rules out the obvious algorithm
an invariant, parity, or bound never changes no matter what you do
“minimum operations” where each operation has one clean effect
insight.one_liner: No template. One observation collapses the problem: find what is preserved, what is bounded, or what the extremes force, then the code is a few lines.
template: # 1. play the smallest cases by hand
# 2. name what every operation preserves (sum? parity? order? a bound?)
# 3. the answer is usually a formula on that invariant, or a scan of the extremes

subtopics.name: Invariants, symmetry, extremes
subtopics.recognize: The brute force is obviously too slow and there is no data structure to reach for.
subtopics.solve: Work small cases, look for what never changes, and try thinking backwards from the final state. Case analysis is legitimate: split by the extreme element or by parity, solve each case cleanly.

strings.name: String Algorithms
signals: “find every occurrence of a pattern” or “the string repeats itself”
compare many substrings for equality, faster than O(length) each
the shortest period / longest border of a string
strings.one_liner: Prefix functions and rolling hashes turn substring questions into O(n): a border table answers periodicity and matching, a polynomial hash compares any two substrings in O(1).
template: pi = [0] * len(p)             # pi[i] = longest proper border of p[:i+1]

subtopics.name: KMP & the failure function
subtopics.recognize: Pattern matching in linear time; “shortest string that makes it a repetition”; longest prefix that is also a suffix.
subtopics.solve: Build pi on the pattern (or on pattern + '#' + text). A border of length b means the string has period n - b.
template: return [i - 2 * len(p) for i in range(len(s)) if pi[i] == len(p)]

subtopics.name: Rolling hash
subtopics.recognize: Many substring equality checks, longest duplicate substring, matching after edits.
subtopics.solve: h[i+1] = h[i] * B + s[i] mod M; hash(l..r) = h[r+1] - h[l] * B^(r-l+1). Use a big modulus or two moduli; binary search the length when the property is monotone.

signals: primes, divisors, gcd/lcm, modular arithmetic
“how many ways” with a closed form: C(n, k), stars and bars
answers “modulo 1e9+7”
number-theory.one_liner: A small toolkit does the work: sieve primes once, factorize by trial division up to sqrt(n), Euclid for gcd, and precomputed factorials with modular inverses for C(n, k).
template: for j in range(i * i, n + 1, i):

subtopics.name: Primes, divisors, gcd
subtopics.recognize: Primality, prime factors, count of divisors, gcd of an array, lcm.
subtopics.solve: Sieve when many queries; trial division to sqrt(n) for one number; gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b). Divisor counts come from the factorization: product of (exponent + 1).

subtopics.name: Counting with C(n, k)
subtopics.recognize: Count arrangements, paths on a grid, ways to distribute identical items.
subtopics.solve: Precompute fact[] and inv_fact[] mod p (Fermat inverse). Multiplication principle first, then subtract the forbidden cases (inclusion-exclusion).
template: return fact[a] * inv[b] % MOD * inv[a - b] % MOD if 0 <= b <= a else 0

fenwick-segment.name: Fenwick & Segment Tree
signals: point updates interleaved with prefix / range queries
“count smaller elements to the right”, inversions
range min / max / sum over an array that changes
fenwick-segment.one_liner: Log-time range queries under updates. A Fenwick tree is ten lines and covers prefix sums and counting; a segment tree generalizes to any associative operation.

subtopics.name: Fenwick tree (BIT)
subtopics.recognize: Prefix sums with point updates; “how many earlier elements are smaller” (compress values, then count).
subtopics.solve: i & -i walks the tree. Inversions: scan left to right, query how many seen values are larger, then insert.

subtopics.name: Segment tree
subtopics.recognize: Range min/max/sum with point updates, or a query the Fenwick tree cannot express.
subtopics.solve: Build over [l, r) recursively; query and update descend into the halves that overlap. Lazy propagation only when range updates are required.
template: build(2 * o, l, m); build(2 * o + 1, m, r)
def query(o, l, r, ql, qr):
if ql <= l and r <= qr: return t[o]
if ql < m: res = merge(res, query(2 * o, l, m, ql, qr))
if qr > m: res = merge(res, query(2 * o + 1, m, r, ql, qr))
